| Control | branch outcome/target unknown | `beq` – fetched instructions may be wrong |

RAW stall without forwarding:

| Cycle | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| add r1 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| sub (uses r1) | | IF | stall | stall | ID | EX |

### Follow-ups
- *Which data hazards occur in a simple in-order 5-stage pipe?* Only RAW; WAR/WAW appear with out-of-order or variable-latency units.

questions.title: What techniques can be used to avoid structural, data and control pipeline hazards?
questions.answer: Structural: duplicate resources (separate I/D caches, multiple execution units, separate load/store units). Data: out-of-order execution, data forwarding. Control: branch prediction.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Structural → duplicate/pipeline resources. Data → forwarding (bypass), out-of-order execution, register renaming, compiler scheduling. Control → branch prediction, delayed branches, early branch resolution.

| Hazard | Techniques |
| --- | --- |
| Structural | separate I$/D$, multiple execution units (INT/FP, load/store), pipelined units, multi-port register files |
| Data (RAW) | forwarding/bypass from EX/MEM/WB, stall (interlock) only when unavoidable (load-use), instruction scheduling |
| Data (WAR/WAW) | register renaming, in-order commit (ROB) |
| Control | static/dynamic branch prediction (BHT, BTB, return stack), speculative execution, branch delay slot, resolve branch in ID |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  EX["EX stage result"] -->|"forward"| MUX["ALU input mux"]
  MEM["MEM stage result"] -->|"forward"| MUX
  RF["register file"] --> MUX
  MUX --> ALU["ALU (dependent instruction)"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Which RAW can't be fully forwarded in a 5-stage pipe?* Load-use: data is available only after MEM → 1-cycle stall.
- *Verification angle:* write directed back-to-back dependency tests and cover every forwarding path × source stage.

questions.title: A pipelined machine has 10 stages, each taking 1 ns. Assuming no hazards, how long does it take to process 100 data elements?
questions.answer: First element takes 10 ns, remaining 99 take 1 ns each: 10 + 99 = 109 ns.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The first element needs the full pipeline latency (10 ns); after that one element completes every cycle. Total = (k + n − 1) × t = (10 + 99) × 1 ns = **109 ns**.

| Element | Completes at |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 10 ns (pipeline fill) |
| 2 | 11 ns |
| … | … |
| 100 | 10 + 99 = **109 ns** |

```mermaid
gantt
  title First elements in a 10-stage pipeline (1 ns per stage)
  dateFormat X
  axisFormat %s
  section Element 1
  Stages 1-10 :0, 10
  section Element 2
  Stages 1-10 :1, 11
  section Element 100
  Stages 1-10 :99, 109
```

### Explanation
- Non-pipelined: 100 × 10 ns = 1000 ns → speedup = 1000/109 ≈ 9.2× (approaches 10× as n → ∞).

### Follow-ups
- *Throughput in steady state?* 1 element/ns = 1 G elements/s.

questions.title: What are the different types of addressing modes for an instruction?
questions.answer: Immediate (operand in instruction), direct (address in instruction), register (operands in registers), indexed (base register + offset).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The addressing mode defines how an instruction finds its operand: as a constant in the instruction, in a register, at a fixed address, or at an address computed from registers.

| Mode | Example | Operand / effective address |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate | `add r0, r1, #0x12` | constant 0x12 in the instruction |
| Register | `mul r0, r1, r2` | contents of r1, r2 |
| Direct (absolute) | `load r0, 0x10000` | mem[0x10000] |
| Register indirect | `load r0, [r1]` | mem[r1] |
| Indexed / base+offset | `load r0, [r1 + 8]` | mem[r1 + 8] |
| PC-relative | `beq label` | PC + offset |
| Auto-increment | `load r0, [r1]+` | mem[r1], then r1 += size |

### Explanation
- RISC ISAs keep few modes (register, immediate, base+offset, PC-relative); CISC ISAs offer many.
- Indexed mode is how arrays/structs are accessed (base register + offset).

### Follow-ups
- *Which mode does a jump table use?* Indexed/indirect.

questions.title: What is the principle of spatial and temporal locality of reference?
questions.answer: Temporal locality: a recently referenced location is likely to be referenced again soon. Spatial locality: locations near a recently referenced location are likely to be referenced soon.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Temporal locality**: a location accessed now is likely to be accessed again soon (loop variables, stack). **Spatial locality**: locations near a recently accessed one are likely to be accessed soon (arrays, sequential code). Caches exploit both: keep recent data (temporal) and fetch whole lines (spatial).

```c
int sum = 0;                    /* 'sum' and 'i': temporal locality */
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
    sum += a[i];                /* a[0], a[1], ... : spatial locality */
```

| Access trace | Locality |
| --- | --- |
| 0x100, 0x100, 0x100 | temporal |
| 0x100, 0x104, 0x108, 0x10C | spatial |
| 0x100, 0x9000, 0x4400 | neither (cache-unfriendly) |

### Follow-ups
- *Row-major array traversed by column?* Poor spatial locality – stride equals the row size, so each access may miss.

questions.title: What are the different kinds of memories in a system?
questions.answer: Registers, cache, main/primary memory, and secondary memory (magnetic/optical).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Memory is a hierarchy trading speed for capacity and cost: registers → caches → main memory → secondary storage.

| Level | Technology | Typical size | Typical latency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registers | flip-flops | < 1 KB | < 1 cycle |
| Cache (L1/L2/L3) | SRAM | KB – tens of MB | 1–40 cycles |
| Main/primary memory | DRAM | GB | ~100 cycles |
| Secondary memory | Flash/SSD, magnetic disk, optical | TB | µs – ms |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  R["Registers"] --> C["Cache (SRAM)"] --> M["Main memory (DRAM)"] --> S["Secondary storage (SSD/HDD/optical)"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Which are volatile?* Registers, caches, DRAM; secondary storage is non-volatile.

questions.title: What is a cache?
questions.answer: A cache is a small amount of fast memory between main memory and the CPU (often on the CPU chip).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A cache is a small, fast memory (SRAM) between the CPU and main memory that holds copies of recently/nearby used memory blocks so most accesses avoid slow DRAM.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CPU["CPU"] <-->|"word transfer (fast)"| CACHE["cache"]
  CACHE <-->|"block / line transfer (slow)"| MEM["main memory"]
```

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Line/block | unit of transfer (e.g., 64 B) |
| Tag | identifies which memory block is in a line |
| Valid / dirty bits | line holds data / line modified (write-back) |
| Hit / miss | data found / not found in cache |

### Explanation
- Average memory access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; e.g., 1 + 0.05 × 100 = 6 cycles vs 100 without a cache.

### Follow-ups
- *Where is the cache?* On the CPU die (L1/L2 per core, shared L3), sometimes off-chip.

questions.title: Give an overview of cache operation. What is the principle behind the functioning of a cache?
questions.answer: CPU checks cache first; on a hit data comes from cache. On a miss, a block is read from main memory into the cache and delivered to the CPU. Tags identify which memory block is in each slot. Based on locality of reference.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** On every access the cache is checked first (tag compare). Hit → data returned quickly. Miss → the whole block containing the address is fetched from memory into a cache line (evicting another if needed), then delivered. It works because of **locality of reference**.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["CPU read address"] --> B{"tag match and valid?"}
  B -->|"hit"| C["return data from cache"]
  B -->|"miss"| D["choose victim line (LRU etc.)"]
  D --> E{"victim dirty?"}
  E -->|"yes"| F["write victim back to memory"]
  E -->|"no"| G["fetch block from memory"]
  F --> G
  G --> H["fill line, update tag/valid"] --> C
```

| Address field | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| Offset | byte within line |
| Index | which set |
| Tag | compared with stored tag |

### Follow-ups
- *Write policies?* Write-through vs write-back; write-allocate vs no-write-allocate.

questions.title: What is a cache hit and a cache miss?
questions.answer: A cache hit is when the looked-up address is present in the cache; a miss is when it is not found.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Hit**: the requested address is present (valid line with matching tag) in the cache. **Miss**: it is not, so the block must be fetched from the next level.

| Access (direct-mapped, 4 lines, 1-word lines) | Index | Result | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| addr 0 | 0 | miss | cold/compulsory |
| addr 1 | 1 | miss | cold |
| addr 0 | 0 | **hit** | already cached |
| addr 4 | 0 | miss | conflict – evicts addr 0 |
| addr 0 | 0 | miss | conflict |

### Explanation
- Miss types (3 Cs): **compulsory** (first touch), **capacity** (working set > cache), **conflict** (too many blocks map to one set).
- Hit rate = hits / accesses; here 1/5.

### Follow-ups
- *How to reduce conflict misses?* Higher associativity or a victim cache.

questions.title: Will a program that searches a value in a linked list perform differently from one that searches a vector on a machine with a cache?
questions.answer: Yes: vector elements are contiguous, so cache-line fills bring adjacent elements and search is faster; linked-list nodes are non-contiguous and cause more misses.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Yes. A vector is **contiguous**, so each cache-line fill (64–128 B) brings in many following elements (spatial locality) and hardware prefetchers detect the stride. Linked-list nodes are scattered, so almost every node visit can be a cache miss (pointer chasing). Vector search is faster.

| Aspect | Vector / array | Linked list |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layout | contiguous | scattered heap nodes |
| Elements per 64 B line (4-B ints) | 16 | ~1 (plus pointer overhead) |
| Misses for 1024 elements (cold) | ~64 | up to ~1024 |
| Prefetching | effective (sequential) | ineffective (next address unknown until load completes) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Vector
    L1["line: e0..e15"] --> L2["line: e16..e31"] --> L3["..."]
  end
  subgraph List
    N1["node @0x1000"] --> N2["node @0x8A40"] --> N3["node @0x3310"] --> N4["..."]
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Both are O(n) – why care?* Constant factors: a DRAM miss costs ~100+ cycles, so the list can be 10× slower.

questions.title: What are the different mechanisms for mapping memory to caches? Compare their advantages and disadvantages.
questions.answer: Direct mapping: block k maps to cache block k mod N (simple, one tag compare, but conflict evictions). Fully associative: any block anywhere (best utilization, but compares all tags – big, power hungry). Set associative: direct map to a set, any way within set (compromise). E.g., 64B line, 128 blocks, 32-bit address: direct = offset[5:0], index[12:6], tag[31:13]; 2-way 64 sets: index[11:6], tag[31:12].
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Direct-mapped**: each memory block maps to exactly one line (block k → line k mod N). **Fully associative**: any block can go to any line. **N-way set-associative**: block maps to one set (k mod #sets) and to any way within it – the usual compromise.

Example: 32-bit address, 64 B lines, 128 lines (8 KB cache):

| Mapping | Tag | Index | Offset | Tag compares per lookup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct-mapped (128 sets × 1) | [31:13] (19 b) | [12:6] (7 b) | [5:0] | 1 |
| 2-way (64 sets × 2) | [31:12] (20 b) | [11:6] (6 b) | [5:0] | 2 |
| Fully associative (1 set × 128) | [31:6] (26 b) | none | [5:0] | 128 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ADDR["address"] --> T["tag"]
  ADDR --> I["index → select set"]
  ADDR --> O["offset → byte in line"]
  I --> SET["set: way0 tag | way1 tag"]
  T --> CMP["parallel compare with each way"]
  SET --> CMP --> HIT["hit/miss + way select"]
```

| Mapping | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct | simplest, fastest hit, 1 comparator, lowest power | conflict misses (thrashing) even when cache is not full |
| Fully associative | no conflict misses, best utilization | N comparators, slow/power hungry, complex replacement; only for small structures (TLBs) |
| Set-associative | balances conflict misses vs cost | more comparators/muxing than direct; replacement policy needed |

### Follow-ups
- *Which addresses conflict in the direct-mapped example?* Any two whose bits [12:6] match, e.g., 0x0000 and 0x2000.

questions.title: What is the disadvantage of having a cache with more associativity?
questions.answer: More associativity needs bigger comparator logic to compare against tags in all ways of a set: more power and more hardware.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** More ways per set means more tags to compare **in parallel** on every lookup: more comparators, wider way-select muxes, more complex replacement state → more area, power and often a longer hit latency. Returns diminish beyond ~8–16 ways.

| Associativity (256 KB, 64 B lines) | Sets | Tag comparators per lookup | Conflict misses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1-way (direct) | 4096 | 1 | highest |
| 4-way | 1024 | 4 | lower |
| 16-way | 256 | 16 | lower still |
| Fully associative | 1 | 4096 | none |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  IDX["index"] --> W0["way0 tag"]
  IDX --> W1["way1 tag"]
  IDX --> WN["... wayN-1 tag"]
  W0 --> C0["=?"]
  W1 --> C1["=?"]
  WN --> CN["=?"]
  C0 --> HIT["OR → hit, N:1 data mux"]
  C1 --> HIT
  CN --> HIT
```

### Follow-ups
- *Replacement cost?* True LRU for N ways needs log2(N!) bits/set – why tree-PLRU is used.

questions.title: A byte-addressable CPU with a 16-bit address bus has a direct-mapped cache with 1-byte blocks and a 4-bit index. How many blocks does the cache hold, and how many tag bits are stored per block?
questions.answer: 4-bit index → 16 blocks; address[3:0] is the index and address[15:4] (12 bits) is the tag.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Index bits select the line: 4 bits → 2^4 = **16 blocks**. Block size 1 B → 0 offset bits. Tag = 16 − 4 − 0 = **12 bits** (addr[15:4]).

| Field | Bits | Width |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tag | [15:4] | 12 |
| Index | [3:0] | 4 |
| Offset | – | 0 |

Worked example: address 0xA3C7 → index = 0x7 (line 7), tag = 0xA3C.

### Follow-ups
- *Total storage including valid bit?* 16 × (8 data + 12 tag + 1 valid) = 336 bits.

questions.title: A 4-way set-associative cache is 256 KB with 64-byte lines. How many sets are there, and how many tag bits are needed for a 32-bit address?
questions.answer: 4096 lines / 4 ways = 1024 sets. Offset [5:0], set index [15:6] (10 bits), tag [31:16] (16 bits).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Lines = 256 KB / 64 B = 4096; sets = 4096 / 4 = **1024** → 10 index bits. Offset = log2 64 = 6 bits. Tag = 32 − 10 − 6 = **16 bits**.

| Field | Address bits | Width |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tag | [31:16] | 16 |
| Set index | [15:6] | 10 |
| Offset | [5:0] | 6 |

| Step | Calculation |
| --- | --- |
| Lines | 2^18 / 2^6 = 2^12 = 4096 |
| Sets | 4096 / 4 = 1024 = 2^10 |
| Tag bits | 32 − 10 − 6 = 16 |

### Follow-ups
- *8-way instead?* 512 sets → 9 index bits → 17 tag bits.
- *Tag array size?* 4096 lines × 16 bits = 64 Kbit (+ valid/dirty/LRU bits).

questions.title: What is the difference between write-through and write-back caches? What are the advantages and disadvantages?
questions.answer: Write-through writes every cache write to main memory too (simple, memory always up to date, but uses bandwidth). Write-back writes only to cache and defers memory update until eviction (saves bandwidth, but coherency is more complex).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Write-through**: every write updates the cache **and** memory (memory always current, costs bandwidth). **Write-back**: writes update only the cache and mark the line **dirty**; memory is updated on eviction (saves bandwidth, needs dirty tracking and coherence care).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CPU
  participant Cache
  participant Mem as Memory
  Note over CPU,Mem: Write-through
  CPU->>Cache: write A=5
  Cache->>Mem: write A=5 (every time)
  Note over CPU,Mem: Write-back
  CPU->>Cache: write A=5 (dirty=1)
  CPU->>Cache: write A=6 (still dirty)
  Cache->>Mem: write back A=6 (only on eviction)
```

| Aspect | Write-through | Write-back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Memory up to date | always | only after eviction |
| Memory bandwidth | high (every store) | low (once per dirty line) |
| Complexity | simple (often + write buffer) | dirty bits, write-back on eviction |
| Coherence / I/O | simple | must snoop/flush dirty lines |
| Eviction cost | none | may require write-back |

### Follow-ups
- *Write-allocate?* On a write miss, fetch the line then write (usually paired with write-back); no-write-allocate pairs with write-through.

questions.title: What is the difference between an inclusive and an exclusive cache?
questions.answer: Inclusive: all L1 addresses are also in L2. Exclusive: an address is in at most one of L1/L2. Exclusive stores more data overall; inclusive makes snooping easier (only check L2).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In a multi-level hierarchy, **inclusive**: every line in L1 is also in L2. **Exclusive**: a line lives in at most one of L1/L2. (Non-inclusive/NINE: no guarantee either way.)

| Aspect | Inclusive | Exclusive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effective capacity | L2 only (L1 duplicated) | L1 + L2 |
| Snoop filtering | check L2 only – miss in L2 means not in L1 | must check L1 and L2 |
| L2 eviction | must back-invalidate L1 copy | no back-invalidation |
| L1 eviction | just drop (copy in L2) | victim moves into L2 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Inclusive
    L1a["L1: A B"] --- L2a["L2: A B C D"]
  end
  subgraph Exclusive
    L1b["L1: A B"] --- L2b["L2: C D E F"]
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Verification checks?* For inclusive caches, assert that every valid L1 tag exists in L2 (a great scoreboard/assertion invariant).

questions.title: What are the different algorithms used for cache line replacement in a set-associative cache?
questions.answer: LRU (age bits), MRU, Pseudo-LRU (one or two bits), LFU (frequency counts), Random replacement.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** When a set is full the replacement policy picks a victim: LRU, pseudo-LRU, MRU, LFU, FIFO/round-robin or random.

| Policy | State per set | Idea | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LRU | age bits per line | evict least recently used | best for temporal locality, costly for many ways |
| Pseudo-LRU (tree) | N−1 bits | binary tree points away from recently used | cheap approximation |
| MRU | age bits | evict most recently used | good for cyclic scans larger than the cache |
| LFU | counters | evict least frequently used | needs aging to adapt |
| FIFO / round-robin | pointer | evict oldest filled | simple |
| Random | LFSR | evict random way | no state, surprisingly good |

Worked LRU trace (2-way set, accesses A B A C):

| Access | Way0 | Way1 | LRU after | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | A | – | way1 | miss |
| B | A | B | way0 | miss |
| A | A | B | way1 | hit |
| C | A | **C** (evict B) | way0 | miss |

### Follow-ups
- *Tree-PLRU for 4 ways?* 3 bits: root picks a pair, child bit picks a way within the pair; on access, flip bits to point away.

questions.title: What is the cache coherency problem?
questions.answer: In SMP systems, multiple caches can hold copies of the same address; if processors update freely, reads on different processors can see different values – inconsistent view of memory.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In a shared-memory multiprocessor each core has a private cache, so the **same address can have multiple copies**. If cores update their copies independently, different cores see different values for one location – an inconsistent view of memory.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P0 as P0 cache
  participant M as Memory (X=0)
  participant P1 as P1 cache
  P0->>M: read X → caches 0
  P1->>M: read X → caches 0
  P0->>P0: write X=1 (write-back, local only)
  P1->>P1: read X → still 0 (stale!)
```

| Requirement | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Write propagation | a write must eventually be visible to all cores |
| Write serialization | all cores see writes to one address in the same order |

### Explanation
- Solved by hardware coherence protocols (MESI/MOESI) using snooping or directories; software alternatives are cache flush/invalidate.

### Follow-ups
- *Coherence vs consistency?* Coherence concerns one address; memory consistency concerns ordering across different addresses.

questions.title: What is the difference between snoop-based and directory-based cache coherency protocols?
questions.answer: Snoop: requests broadcast to all processors, each snoops and responds – faster for small systems but doesn't scale. Directory: a directory tracks which processors cache which addresses; point-to-point requests – longer latency but scales better.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Snoop-based**: every request is **broadcast**; all caches snoop and respond. **Directory-based**: a directory tracks which caches hold each line; requests go to the directory, which sends **point-to-point** messages only to sharers.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Snoop
    P0["P0"] -->|"broadcast"| BUS["shared bus / ring"]
    BUS --> P1["P1"]
    BUS --> P2["P2"]
    BUS --> P3["P3"]
  end
  subgraph Directory
    Q0["P0"] -->|"request"| DIR["directory: line X → {P2}"]
    DIR -->|"point-to-point"| Q2["P2"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Snoop-based | Directory-based |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Messaging | broadcast | targeted |
| Latency (small system) | low | extra directory lookup |
| Scalability | poor – traffic grows with cores | good – large SMP/NUMA |
| Storage | none extra | directory entries (presence bits) |

### Follow-ups
- *Hybrid?* Snoop filters: an inclusive tag directory filters broadcasts.

questions.title: What is the MESI protocol?
questions.answer: MESI: per-line states Modified (dirty), Exclusive (clean, only copy, can be written), Shared (clean, multiple copies, no write), Invalid. Reads serviced in any state except I; writes only in M or E.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** MESI is a write-back cache-coherence protocol with four per-line states: **M**odified (dirty, only copy), **E**xclusive (clean, only copy), **S**hared (clean, maybe other copies), **I**nvalid. Reads are serviced in M/E/S; writes only in M/E (S must first invalidate others).

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  I --> E: local read, no other sharer
  I --> S: local read, others have it
  I --> M: local write (RFO)
  E --> M: local write (silent)
  E --> S: snoop read
  S --> M: local write (invalidate others)
  M --> S: snoop read (supply data, write back)
  M --> I: snoop write / RFO
  S --> I: snoop write / RFO
  E --> I: snoop write / RFO
```

| State | Dirty? | Other copies? | Can read | Can write |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | yes | no | yes | yes |
| E | no | no | yes | yes (→ M silently) |
| S | no | possibly | yes | no – upgrade first |
| I | – | – | no | no |

### Follow-ups
- *Why E?* Lets a private line be written without a bus transaction – the main gain over MSI.

questions.title: What are the MESIF and MOESI(F) protocols?
questions.answer: Extensions of MESI. F (Forward): specialized S state; one cache is designated responder to forward data, reducing memory traffic. O (Owned): allows dirty data to be shared among caches without writing back to memory (line goes M→O when shared).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Extensions of MESI. **F (Forward)** – one designated sharer of a clean shared line answers requests with data (cache-to-cache), cutting memory traffic (Intel MESIF). **O (Owned)** – a dirty line can be shared; the owner supplies data and is responsible for the eventual write-back, deferring the memory write (AMD MOESI).

| State | Dirty | Shared | Responds with data |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M | yes | no | yes |
| O | yes | yes (others in S) | yes – owner |
| E | no | no | yes |
| S | no | yes | no |
| F | no | yes | yes – designated forwarder |
| I | – | – | no |

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  M --> O: snoop read (share dirty data, no memory write)
  O --> M: local write (invalidate sharers)
  O --> I: snoop invalidate
  S --> F: becomes designated forwarder
  F --> S: forwarding duty passed to new requester
```

### Follow-ups
- *In MESIF, who gets F after a forward?* Usually the newest requester (most likely to keep the line).

questions.title: What is an RFO (Read For Ownership)?
questions.answer: RFO = Read For Ownership: a read with intent to write; combines read and invalidate broadcast, issued when writing to a line in S or I state; others invalidate their copies.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** RFO is a coherence transaction = **read + invalidate**. A core that wants to write a line it holds in S or I issues an RFO; it obtains the latest data and all other caches invalidate their copies, so the requester gets the line in E/M.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P0 as P0 (line in I)
  participant IC as Interconnect
  participant P1 as P1 (line in S)
  participant P2 as P2 (line in M)
  P0->>IC: RFO(X)
  IC->>P1: snoop invalidate
  IC->>P2: snoop invalidate
  P1-->>IC: ack (S→I)
  P2-->>IC: data (M→I)
  IC-->>P0: data, exclusive
  Note over P0: P0 writes X, state M
```

### Explanation
- If the requester already has valid data in S, an **upgrade** (invalidate-only) can be used instead of a full RFO.
- Write-heavy sharing causes RFO "ping-pong" (false sharing when different variables share a line).

### Follow-ups
- *How would you verify RFO?* Check that after completion no other cache holds the line valid, and data returned is the latest (scoreboard against a memory model).

questions.title: What is the concept of virtual memory?
questions.answer: Virtual memory lets a processor see a contiguous virtual address space even with small physical memory; OS manages mapping (paging) between virtual space, physical memory and secondary storage; MMU translates virtual to physical addresses.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Each process sees a large, private, contiguous **virtual address space**; the OS and the MMU map virtual **pages** to physical frames (or to disk), so programs can be larger than physical RAM and are isolated from each other.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph VA["Process virtual pages"]
    V0["VP0"]
    V1["VP1"]
    V2["VP2"]
    V3["VP3"]
  end
  V0 --> F5["PF5"]
  V1 --> F1["PF1"]
  V2 --> DISK["on disk (swap)"]
  V3 --> F7["PF7"]
  subgraph PM["Physical memory frames"]
    F1
    F5
    F7
  end
```

| Benefit | How |
| --- | --- |
| Larger than RAM | inactive pages live on disk |
| Isolation/protection | per-process page tables, permission bits |
| Simplified linking/loading | every process starts at the same virtual addresses |
| Sharing | map the same frame into multiple processes |

### Follow-ups
- *Hardware involved?* MMU, TLB, page-table walker; page faults handled by the OS.

questions.title: What is the difference between a virtual memory address and a physical memory address?
questions.answer: Virtual address: used by a program/process within its address space. Physical address: the actual DRAM location after OS/hardware translation via paging; missing pages are brought from disk.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A **virtual address** is what software/processes use; a **physical address** is what actually goes to DRAM. The MMU translates VA → PA through page tables (cached in the TLB); the page offset is unchanged.

| Field (4 KB pages, 32-bit VA) | Bits |
| --- | --- |
| Virtual page number (VPN) | VA[31:12] |
| Page offset | VA[11:0] |
| Physical address | {PFN from page table, VA[11:0]} |

Example: VA 0x0040_3ABC, page table maps VPN 0x00403 → PFN 0x1F2 → PA 0x001F_2ABC.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  VA["VA = VPN | offset"] --> TLB{"TLB hit?"}
  TLB -->|"yes"| PA["PA = PFN | offset"]
  TLB -->|"no"| PT["page table walk"] --> PA
  PT -->|"page not present"| PF["page fault → OS loads from disk"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Can two processes use the same VA?* Yes – they map to different PAs.

questions.title: What is the concept of paging?
questions.answer: Virtual address space is divided into pages (contiguous blocks, usually ≥ 4 KB; large pages 1–4 MB); a page is the minimum unit moved from secondary storage. Page tables translate virtual to physical addresses.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Virtual and physical memory are divided into fixed-size **pages/frames** (typically 4 KB; large pages 2 MB/1 GB). A **page table** maps each virtual page number to a physical frame number plus permission/present bits. The page is the unit moved between disk and memory.

| VPN | Present | PFN | R/W/X |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x000 | 1 | 0x05 | R-X (code) |
| 0x001 | 1 | 0x01 | RW- |
| 0x002 | 0 | – (on disk) | RW- |
| 0x003 | 1 | 0x07 | RW- |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  VA["VA: VPN | offset"] --> PTBR["page table base reg"]
  PTBR --> PTE["PTE[VPN]"] --> PA["PFN | offset"]
```

### Explanation
- No external fragmentation (all pages same size); internal fragmentation in the last page.
- Multi-level page tables keep table memory proportional to used address space.

### Follow-ups
- *Why large pages?* Fewer TLB misses for big working sets.

questions.title: What is a TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)?
questions.answer: A TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical translations; on a hit the physical address is obtained quickly without a page-table walk; on a miss the page tables must be walked in memory.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A TLB is a small (often fully/highly associative) **cache of recent VA→PA translations**. A TLB hit gives the physical address in ~1 cycle; a miss triggers a page-table walk (several memory accesses).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["virtual address"] --> B{"TLB lookup (VPN)"}
  B -->|"hit"| C["PA = PFN | offset → cache/memory"]
  B -->|"miss"| D["page table walk in memory"]
  D -->|"PTE valid"| E["refill TLB"] --> C
  D -->|"not present"| F["page fault exception → OS"]
```

| Event | Typical cost |
| --- | --- |
| TLB hit | 0–1 cycles |
| TLB miss, walk hits caches | 10–50 cycles |
| Page fault | millions of cycles (disk/OS) |

### Follow-ups
- *Context switch issue?* TLB entries belong to a process – flush or tag entries with ASIDs.
- *TLB reach?* entries × page size, e.g., 64 × 4 KB = 256 KB.

questions.title: What is meant by a page fault?
questions.answer: When a page mapped into virtual address space but not loaded in main memory is accessed, the MMU raises an interrupt called a page fault.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A page fault is the exception the MMU raises when a program accesses a page that is mapped in its virtual address space but **not currently present in physical memory** (or violates permissions). The OS handles it: load the page from disk, update the page table, and restart the faulting instruction.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CPU
  participant MMU
  participant OS
  participant Disk
  CPU->>MMU: load VA
  MMU-->>CPU: PTE present=0 → page fault
  CPU->>OS: trap to handler
  OS->>Disk: read page
  Disk-->>OS: page data
  OS->>OS: pick frame (evict if needed), update PTE
  OS-->>CPU: return, re-execute instruction
```

| Type | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| Minor/soft | page in memory but not mapped (e.g., shared/page cache) |
| Major/hard | page must be read from disk |
| Invalid | illegal address/permission → segmentation fault |

### Follow-ups
- *Fault or trap?* A page fault is a **fault** – handled before the instruction completes so it can be restarted.

questions.title: If a CPU is busy executing a task, how can we stop it and run another task?
questions.answer: By using external interrupt sources to interrupt program execution.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Use an **interrupt**. An external (or timer) interrupt makes the CPU finish the current instruction, save context (PC, flags, registers), jump to the interrupt service routine / OS scheduler, which can then switch to another task.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TaskA
  participant CPU
  participant Dev as Timer / device
  participant ISR as ISR / scheduler
  TaskA->>CPU: executing
  Dev->>CPU: IRQ asserted
  CPU->>CPU: finish current instruction, save PC/flags
  CPU->>ISR: vector to handler
  ISR->>ISR: save Task A context, choose Task B
  ISR-->>CPU: restore Task B context, return-from-interrupt
```

### Explanation
- Preemptive multitasking OSes use a periodic timer interrupt for time slicing.
- Interrupts can be masked; non-maskable interrupts (NMI) cannot.

### Follow-ups
- *Polling alternative?* The task itself checks a flag periodically – cooperative, wastes cycles, higher latency.

questions.title: What are interrupts and exceptions, and how are they different?
questions.answer: Interrupts: asynchronous events from external hardware, serviced after the current instruction. Exceptions: synchronous events from instruction execution (divide by zero, undefined instruction); types: faults (serviced before the faulting instruction), traps (after), aborts (severe errors).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Interrupts** are **asynchronous** events from outside the instruction stream (I/O, timers), serviced at an instruction boundary. **Exceptions** are **synchronous** events caused by the executing instruction (divide-by-zero, illegal opcode, page fault). Exceptions are classified as faults, traps and aborts.

| Aspect | Interrupt | Exception |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source | external hardware | current instruction |
| Timing | asynchronous | synchronous, repeatable |
| Examples | keyboard, USB, timer, DMA done | divide by zero, undefined instruction, page fault, breakpoint |

| Exception class | When handled | Return to | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fault | before instruction completes | faulting instruction (re-execute) | page fault |
| Trap | after the instruction | next instruction | breakpoint, syscall |
| Abort | – | no reliable return | machine check, double fault |

### Follow-ups
- *Precise exceptions?* All earlier instructions completed, none later have changed state – required to restart after a fault (ROB in out-of-order CPUs).

questions.title: What is a vectored interrupt?
questions.answer: In a vectored interrupt, the interrupting device sends a unique code that directs the processor to the correct ISR. Non-vectored: first-level ISR reads status registers to decode the source.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** With a **vectored** interrupt the interrupting device supplies a unique code (vector) that directly selects its ISR address (via a vector table). With **non-vectored** interrupts a common handler must read status registers to find the source, then dispatch.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Vectored
    D1["device"] -->|"IRQ + vector 0x21"| VT["vector table[0x21]"] --> ISR1["specific ISR"]
  end
  subgraph NonVectored["Non-vectored"]
    D2["device"] -->|"IRQ"| GH["common handler"] --> RS["read interrupt status reg"] --> ISR2["dispatch to ISR"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Vectored | Non-vectored |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Latency | lower | higher (software decode) |
| Hardware | vector delivery, table | simple |
| Examples | x86 IDT, ARM NVIC | simple MCUs, GIC with software dispatch |

### Follow-ups
- *Verification point?* Check each source maps to the correct vector, priority/nesting, and that pending/clear bits behave per spec.

questions.title: What techniques are used to improve the performance of instruction fetching from memory?
questions.answer: Instruction cache and prefetch (fetch ahead of decode/execute to hide latency) and branch prediction/branch target prediction (keep fetching along the predicted path).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Hide memory latency in the front-end: **instruction cache + prefetching** (fetch ahead of decode) and **branch prediction + branch target prediction** (keep fetching down the predicted path without waiting for execution).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  BP["branch predictor + BTB"] -->|"next PC"| PC["PC"]
  PC --> IC["I-cache"]
  PF["prefetcher (next lines)"] --> IC
  IC --> FQ["fetch queue / buffer"] --> DEC["decode"]
```

| Technique | What it hides |
| --- | --- |
| I-cache | DRAM latency for hot code |
| Sequential prefetch / stream buffers | cold misses for straight-line code |
| Branch direction prediction | wait for branch resolution |
| Branch target buffer (BTB), return stack | wait for target computation |
| Fetch queue / decoupled front-end | short stalls |
| Wider fetch, trace/uop caches | fetch bandwidth |

### Follow-ups
- *Cost of a mispredict?* Flush everything fetched after the branch – roughly the pipeline depth in cycles.

questions.title: What is meant by a superscalar pipelined processor?
questions.answer: A superscalar processor exploits instruction-level parallelism by dispatching multiple instructions per cycle to different execution units; N instructions per cycle = N-way superscalar.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A superscalar processor issues **more than one instruction per cycle** to multiple execution units (instruction-level parallelism). An N-way superscalar can fetch/decode/issue up to N instructions per cycle (ideal IPC = N).

| Cycle → | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I1 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| I2 | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB | |
| I3 | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB |
| I4 | | IF | ID | EX | MEM | WB |

(2-way superscalar: two instructions in each stage per cycle.)

### Explanation
- Requires dependency checking among instructions issued together, multiple register file ports, multiple ALUs/load-store units; usually combined with out-of-order execution.
- Contrast: VLIW relies on the compiler to bundle independent instructions; superscalar does it in hardware.

### Follow-ups
- *Why is real IPC < N?* Dependencies, branch mispredicts, cache misses, limited execution units.

questions.title: What is the difference between in-order and out-of-order execution?
questions.answer: In-order: instructions are fetched, executed and completed in program order; a stall stalls all later instructions. Out-of-order: fetched in order, executed in any order, completed in order; independent instructions can proceed past a stalled one.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **In-order**: instructions fetch, execute and complete in program order – one stall blocks everything behind it. **Out-of-order**: fetch in order, **execute when operands are ready** (any order), **retire/commit in order** – independent instructions bypass a stalled one.

Program: `I1: load r1,[r2]` (cache miss, 10 cycles), `I2: add r3,r1,1` (depends on I1), `I3: mul r4,r5,r6` (independent).

| Model | I3 executes | Total |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In-order | after I1 and I2 | ~12 cycles |
| Out-of-order | immediately, during I1's miss | ~11 cycles (I3 hidden) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F["fetch/decode (in order)"] --> RN["rename"] --> RS["reservation stations"]
  RS -->|"ready operands, any order"| EU["execution units"]
  EU --> ROB["reorder buffer"] -->|"commit in order"| ARF["architectural state"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Why commit in order?* Precise exceptions and correct architectural state on mispredicts.

questions.title: What is the difference between a conditional branch and an unconditional branch instruction?
questions.answer: Unconditional branch always branches (e.g., Jump <offset>). Conditional branch branches only if a condition is true (e.g., beq ra, rb, <offset>), otherwise continues sequentially.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** An **unconditional** branch always changes the program flow (`jump`, `call`, `return`). A **conditional** branch changes flow only if a condition holds (`beq ra, rb, offset` – branch if equal), otherwise execution falls through.

| Instruction | Type | Next PC |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jump L1` | unconditional | L1 always |
| `beq ra, rb, L1` | conditional | L1 if ra == rb, else PC + 4 |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  B{"beq ra, rb, L1"} -->|"ra == rb (taken)"| L1["L1: target"]
  B -->|"ra != rb (not taken)"| N["PC + 4 (fall through)"]
  J["jump L2"] --> L2["L2: target"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Which needs direction prediction?* Conditional; unconditional only needs target prediction (BTB / return stack).

questions.title: What is branch prediction and branch target prediction?
questions.answer: Branch prediction predicts whether a conditional branch will be taken or not; branch target prediction predicts the target of a taken branch/jump before it is computed.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A **branch (direction) predictor** guesses whether a conditional branch is taken or not-taken. A **branch target predictor** (BTB) guesses *where* a taken branch or jump goes, before execution computes it. Together they let fetch continue without stalls.

2-bit saturating counter (per branch history entry):

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  SNT --> WNT: taken
  WNT --> SNT: not taken
  WNT --> WT: taken
  WT --> WNT: not taken
  WT --> ST: taken
  ST --> WT: not taken
  SNT --> SNT: not taken
  ST --> ST: taken
```

| Structure | Predicts | Indexed by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BHT / pattern table (2-bit counters) | taken / not-taken | PC (+ global history in gshare) |
| BTB | target address | PC of branch |
| Return address stack | return targets | call/return pairing |

### Follow-ups
- *Why 2-bit not 1-bit?* A loop branch mispredicts only once per loop exit instead of twice.

questions.title: What is meant by memory-mapped I/O?
questions.answer: MMIO: CPU uses the same address bus for memory and I/O devices; a region of the address map is reserved for device registers, and the device responds when those addresses are accessed.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** With memory-mapped I/O (MMIO), device registers and buffers occupy part of the **system address map**; the CPU accesses them with ordinary load/store instructions on the same address bus, and the device decoding that address responds.

| Address range | Target |
| --- | --- |
| 0x0000_0000 – 0x0000_03FF | UART / timer registers (MMIO) |
| 0x0000_0400 – 0x3FFF_FFFF | reserved / other peripherals |
| 0x4000_0000 – 0xFFFF_FFFF | DRAM |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CPU["CPU load/store"] --> DEC["address decoder / interconnect"]
  DEC -->|"0x0000_0xxx"| UART["UART regs"]
  DEC -->|"0x4000_0000+"| DDR["DRAM"]
```

### Explanation
- Alternative is port-mapped I/O (separate I/O address space and `in/out` instructions, x86).
- MMIO regions must be uncached/strongly-ordered (side effects on read, e.g., read-to-clear status).

### Follow-ups
- *Verification:* register access tests via the bus, address-map/decoder coverage, UVM RAL.

questions.title: What is the advantage of using one-hot encoding in a design?
questions.answer: In one-hot coding, no decode is needed to know the current state (one bit per state, two bits change per transition). Uses more flip-flops but less combinational logic, helping timing-critical logic.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In one-hot encoding exactly one flop is 1 per state, so the current state is known **without decoding** – next-state and output logic are small and fast, at the cost of more flip-flops (N flops for N states). On each transition exactly two bits change (one clears, one sets).

| State | Binary (2 FFs) | One-hot (4 FFs) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IDLE | 00 | 0001 |
| REQ | 01 | 0010 |
| ACK | 10 | 0100 |
| DONE | 11 | 1000 |

### Code
```systemverilog
typedef enum logic [3:0] {IDLE=4'b0001, REQ=4'b0010, ACK=4'b0100, DONE=4'b1000} st_t;
st_t st;
// "is state ACK?" is a single bit, no comparator:
assign ack_out = st[2];
// sanity assertion
assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) $onehot(st));
```

| Aspect | Binary | One-hot |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flops | log2 N | N |
| Decode logic | comparators | single bit |
| Speed | slower | faster (FPGAs love it) |
| Illegal states | few | many (2^N − N) → need recovery |

### Follow-ups
- *Detect corruption?* `$onehot` assertion / parity of state.

questions.title: What is the difference between static and automatic variables, and between local and global variables?
questions.answer: Scope distinguishes local (visible only in its block) and global (visible everywhere). Storage duration distinguishes static (lives for the whole program) and automatic (exists only while the block executes). A local static has local scope but keeps its value across calls.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Two independent properties. **Scope** (local vs global) = *where* a name is visible. **Lifetime/storage duration** (static vs automatic) = *how long* the storage exists. A local static is visible only inside its function but keeps its value across calls.

| Variable | Scope | Lifetime | Copies |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global | whole program / class | whole program | 1 |
| Local automatic | its block/function | each call (re-created) | 1 per call (re-entrant) |
| Local static | its block/function | whole program | 1 shared by all calls |
| Class static member | class | whole program | 1 shared by all objects |

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class test_class;
  int        inst_int;        // one per object, lives as long as the object
  static int global_static;   // one for the class, lives for the whole simulation

  function void compute();
    static    int count;      // local scope, static lifetime: keeps value across calls
    automatic int sum = 0;    // local scope, automatic: fresh each call
    sum   = sum + 1;          // always 1
    count = count + sum;      // 1, 2, 3, ... on successive calls
    $display("sum=%0d count=%0d", sum, count);
  endfunction
endclass
```

| Call # | sum | count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 3 | 1 | 3 |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- In SystemVerilog, functions/tasks in **modules** are static by default (`task automatic` needed for recursion/re-entrancy); class methods are automatic by default.
- Static locals are not thread-safe across concurrent forked calls.

### Follow-ups
- *C equivalent?* `static int count;` inside a function; `static` at file scope means internal linkage instead.

questions.title: What is an inline function?
questions.answer: A function expanded inline at each call (compiler replaces call with body), avoiding call/return overhead; useful for small functions used often (e.g., max in C).

questions.title: What is a regular expression?
questions.answer: A special sequence of characters used to match or find other strings with a special syntax; powerful pattern matching used in Perl, Python, Tcl.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A regular expression is a pattern language for matching/searching/replacing text. It is used heavily in Perl, Python, Tcl, grep/sed – e.g., to parse simulation logs.

| Pattern | Meaning | Example match |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.` | any char | `a.c` → abc |
| `*`, `+`, `?` | 0+, 1+, 0/1 of previous | `ab+` → abbb |
| `[0-9]`, `\d` | digit | 7 |
| `\w`, `\s` | word char, whitespace | x, space |
| `^`, `$` | start, end of line | `^ERROR` |
| `( )` | capture group | `(\d+)` |
| `{m,n}` | repeat m..n | `\d{2,4}` |

### Code (Python – extract UVM errors from a log)
```python
import re
pat = re.compile(r"^UVM_(ERROR|FATAL)\s+(\S+)\((\d+)\)\s+@\s+(\d+):\s+(.*)$")
with open("sim.log") as f:
    for line in f:
        m = pat.match(line)
        if m:
            sev, file, lineno, time, msg = m.groups()
            print(f"{sev} at t={time}: {msg}  ({file}:{lineno})")
```

### Follow-ups
- *Greedy vs non-greedy?* `.*` grabs as much as possible; `.*?` as little as possible.

questions.title: What is the difference between a heap and a stack?
questions.answer: Stack: stores temporary/local variables of functions, managed automatically, LIFO, limited size (stack overflow). Heap: memory managed by programmer/GC (allocate/free), slower, accessed via pointers, resizable, can fragment.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The **stack** holds function call frames (local automatic variables, return addresses) – allocated/freed automatically in LIFO order, fast, limited size. The **heap** holds dynamically allocated memory (`malloc`/`new`, objects) – managed by the programmer or a garbage collector, larger, slower, accessed through pointers, can fragment.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph Memory["Process address space"]
    TEXT["code (text)"]
    DATA["globals/static (data, bss)"]
    HEAP["heap ↓ grows up: malloc/new"]
    FREE["free space"]
    STACK["stack ↑ grows down: frames"]
  end
  TEXT --- DATA --- HEAP --- FREE --- STACK
```

| Aspect | Stack | Heap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allocation | automatic on function entry | explicit (`malloc`/`new`) |
| Deallocation | automatic on return | `free`/`delete` or GC |
| Speed | very fast (pointer bump) | slower (allocator) |
| Size | small, fixed (stack overflow) | large, can grow |
| Lifetime | until function returns | until freed |
| Fragmentation | none | possible |
| Typical contents | locals, args, return address | objects, dynamic arrays |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Returning a pointer to a local (stack) variable → dangling pointer.
- Deep recursion → stack overflow.

### Follow-ups
- *Where do SV class objects live?* On the simulator's heap; handles are references, memory is garbage-collected.

questions.title: What is the difference between ++a and a++?
questions.answer: ++a increments first and returns the new value; a++ returns the current value and then increments.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Both increment `a`. **Pre-increment `++a`** increments first and yields the new value; **post-increment `a++`** yields the old value, then increments.

### Code (C)
```c
int a = 5, x, y;
x = ++a;   /* a = 6, x = 6 */
y = a++;   /* y = 6, a = 7 */
```

| Statement | a before | value used | a after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `x = ++a;` | 5 | 6 | 6 |
| `y = a++;` | 6 | 6 | 7 |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `i = i++ + ++i;` is undefined behavior in C/C++ (unsequenced modifications).
- In C++, prefer `++it` for iterators/objects (post-increment must copy the old value).
- SystemVerilog supports both too (`i++` in loops), with the same semantics.

questions.title: What is meant by a memory leak?
questions.answer: A memory leak occurs when dynamically allocated memory becomes unreachable without being freed (e.g., C++ objects not deleted). Languages with garbage collection (SystemVerilog, Java) are less prone.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A memory leak happens when dynamically allocated memory is no longer reachable (the last pointer to it is lost) but was never freed, so it can't be reused. Common in C/C++; garbage-collected languages (SystemVerilog, Java, Python) reclaim unreachable objects automatically.

### Code (C++)
```cpp
#include <vector>
void leak() {
    int *p = new int[100];
    p = new int[100];        // first block now unreachable -> leaked
    delete[] p;              // frees only the second block
}
void no_leak() {
    std::vector<int> v(100); // RAII: freed automatically when v goes out of scope
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["pointer p"] -.->|"overwritten"| B1["block #1 (unreachable, leaked)"]
  P --> B2["block #2"]
```

### Explanation
- Detect with valgrind/ASan; avoid with RAII and smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`).
- In SV testbenches, "leaks" still occur when handles are kept in queues/associative arrays forever (e.g., scoreboard never pops matched items) – memory grows over a long simulation.

### Follow-ups
- *Dangling pointer vs leak?* Dangling = pointer to freed memory; leak = allocated memory with no pointer.

questions.title: What is the difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
questions.answer: Compiler translates the whole program into machine code before execution (more analysis time, faster execution, errors after full scan; C/C++). Interpreter translates one statement at a time (less analysis time, slower execution, stops at first error; Perl/Python).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A **compiler** translates the whole program into machine code ahead of time (then the hardware runs it fast). An **interpreter** translates/executes one statement at a time at runtime (slower, but immediate feedback, portable).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Compiler
    S1["source (C/C++)"] --> C["compiler"] --> B["machine code binary"] --> H["CPU executes"]
  end
  subgraph Interpreter
    S2["source (Perl/Python)"] --> I["interpreter (statement by statement / bytecode VM)"] --> H2["CPU runs interpreter"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Compiler | Interpreter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Translation unit | entire program | one statement at a time |
| Analysis time | longer | shorter |
| Output | machine-specific binary | no binary (or intermediate bytecode) |
| Execution speed | faster | slower |
| Errors reported | after scanning whole program | stops at first error |
| Examples | C, C++ | Perl, Python, Tcl |

### Follow-ups
- *Where do HDL simulators fit?* Modern simulators compile HDL to native code (compiled-code simulation); Python is compiled to bytecode then interpreted; JITs blur the line.

questions.title: What is the difference between a statically typed language and a dynamically typed language?
questions.answer: Statically typed: types fixed at compile time, variables declared with types before use (C, Java, SystemVerilog). Dynamically typed: types discovered at execution time (Python, VBScript).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Static typing**: variable types are fixed and checked at compile time (declare before use) – C, C++, Java, SystemVerilog. **Dynamic typing**: types are attached to values and determined at run time – Python, Perl, VBScript.

### Code
```c
/* C: static */
int count = 5;
count = "five";      /* compile-time error */
```
```python
# Python: dynamic
count = 5
count = "five"       # fine - the name now refers to a str
print(count + 1)     # TypeError only when this line runs
```

| Aspect | Static | Dynamic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type errors found | compile time | run time |
| Declarations | required | not required |
| Performance | typically faster | slower (runtime checks) |
| Flexibility | less | more (duck typing) |

### Follow-ups
- *Strong vs weak typing?* A different axis – whether implicit conversions are allowed (Python is dynamic but strong; C is static but fairly weak).

questions.title: Which of the following is false about a stack? (1) Only push and pop apply (2) A stack implements a FIFO (3) Stacks are useful for nested loops and subroutine calls (4) Stacks are efficient for arithmetic expression evaluation
questions.answer: Option (2) is false: a stack is LIFO, not FIFO.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **(2) is false** – a stack is **LIFO** (last in, first out), not FIFO. A queue is FIFO.

| Operation sequence | Stack (LIFO) pops | Queue (FIFO) pops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| push 1, push 2, push 3 | 3, 2, 1 | 1, 2, 3 |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  P["push 3 / pop → 3 (top)"] --> T2["2"] --> T1["1 (bottom)"]
```

### Code (SystemVerilog queue as a stack)
```systemverilog
int stk[$];
initial begin
  stk.push_back(1); stk.push_back(2); stk.push_back(3);
  $display("%0d", stk.pop_back());   // 3 - LIFO
end
```

### Explanation
- Stacks naturally handle nested calls (return addresses), nested loops/parentheses, and postfix (RPN) expression evaluation.

questions.title: What are the major differences between use and require in Perl?
questions.answer: use is evaluated at compile time and implicitly calls import; require is evaluated at run time and doesn't import; use takes only a bareword while require can take a bareword or expression.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `use` is processed at **compile time** and calls the module's `import` (exporting symbols); `require` happens at **run time**, doesn't import, and can take an expression/file path – useful for conditional loading.

| Aspect | `use Module;` | `require Module;` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | compile time (`BEGIN` block) | run time |
| Calls `import` | yes | no |
| Argument | bareword only | bareword or expression (`require $file;`) |
| Failure | script won't compile | dies when executed (can be trapped with `eval`) |

### Code
```perl
use strict;
use List::Util qw(max);          # compile-time, imports max()
print max(3, 9, 4), "\n";

if ($ENV{USE_JSON}) {
    require JSON::PP;             # loaded only if needed, at run time
    print JSON::PP->new->encode({a => 1}), "\n";   # no import: use full name
}
```
- `use Module LIST;` is equivalent to `BEGIN { require Module; Module->import(LIST); }`.

### Follow-ups
- *Load a module only if installed?* `eval { require Foo; 1 } or warn "Foo missing";`

questions.title: What is the difference between static and dynamic memory allocation?
questions.answer: Static: allocated at compile time (stack/other sections), no need to free, fixed size, faster. Dynamic: allocated at run time on the heap, must be freed explicitly, resizable (realloc), slower.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Static** allocation: size fixed at compile time, memory in data segment/stack, freed automatically. **Dynamic** allocation: requested at run time from the heap (`malloc/new`), size can vary, must be freed explicitly.

| Aspect | Static | Dynamic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When allocated | compile/load time | run time |
| Where | data segment or stack | heap |
| Freeing | automatic | explicit (`free`/`delete`) or GC |
| Size change | fixed | resizable (`realloc`) |
| Speed | faster | slower |

### Code (C)
```c
#include <stdlib.h>
int table[256];                       /* static: fixed size */
void f(int n) {
    int *buf = malloc(n * sizeof *buf);  /* dynamic: size known only at run time */
    if (!buf) return;
    buf = realloc(buf, 2 * n * sizeof *buf);
    free(buf);
}
```

### Follow-ups
- *SV analogue?* Fixed-size arrays (static) vs dynamic arrays `new[n]`, queues, associative arrays, class objects (dynamic).

questions.title: What are pre-processor directives?
questions.answer: Lines starting with # are directives to the pre-processor, which modifies the source code before compilation; e.g., #define identifier value replaces identifier with value.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Lines beginning with `#` are instructions to the **pre-processor**, which rewrites the source (macro substitution, file inclusion, conditional compilation) **before** compilation.

| Directive | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `#define N 16` | text/macro substitution |
| `#include "file.h"` | paste another file |
| `#ifdef/#ifndef/#if/#else/#endif` | conditional compilation |
| `#undef` | remove macro |
| `#pragma` | compiler-specific hints |

### Code (C)
```c
#ifndef FIFO_H            /* include guard */
#define FIFO_H
#define DEPTH 16
#define SQR(x) ((x) * (x))   /* parenthesize macro args! */
#ifdef DEBUG
#define LOG(msg) printf("%s\n", msg)
#else
#define LOG(msg)
#endif
#endif
```

### Follow-ups
- *SystemVerilog equivalent?* Compiler directives with a backtick: `` `define``, `` `include``, `` `ifdef``, `` `timescale``.

questions.title: What is the function of 'using namespace std' in C++ code?
questions.answer: A namespace groups entities under a name; std is the standard namespace containing the C++ library (string, cin, cout, vector). 'using namespace std' tells the compiler to use names from the standard library without the std:: prefix.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The C++ standard library (string, vector, cout, cin…) lives in namespace `std`. `using namespace std;` imports all those names into the current scope so you can write `cout` instead of `std::cout`.

### Code
```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;          // bring std:: names into scope
int main() {
    vector<int> v{1, 2, 3};   // instead of std::vector
    cout << v.size() << endl; // instead of std::cout / std::endl
}
```

| Style | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `using namespace std;` | short code | name clashes; never put it in headers |
| `using std::cout;` | selective | a little more typing |
| `std::cout` everywhere | explicit, safe | verbose |

### Follow-ups
- *Why do namespaces exist?* To group related names and avoid collisions between libraries (like SV packages).

questions.title: What is the difference between 'int a;' and 'const int a;'?
questions.answer: int a can be changed at different times in the program; const int a cannot be changed once initialized.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `int a;` is a modifiable variable. `const int a = …;` is read-only after initialization – any later assignment is a compile error (and a const must be initialized at definition).

### Code
```cpp
int a;            // can be assigned any time
a = 5; a = 7;     // OK

const int b = 10; // must be initialized
// b = 11;        // error: assignment of read-only variable 'b'

const int *p1 = &b;   // pointer to const int: *p1 can't change, p1 can
int *const p2 = &a;   // const pointer to int: p2 can't change, *p2 can
```

| Declaration | Can change value? | Can change pointer? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int a` | yes | – |
| `const int a` | no | – |
| `const int *p` | no (*p) | yes |
| `int *const p` | yes (*p) | no |

### Follow-ups
- *SV equivalent?* `const int` / `localparam`; class property `const` can be set once in the constructor.

questions.title: What does the keyword volatile mean in C?
questions.answer: volatile tells the compiler the variable may change between accesses, so it must not optimize accesses (no caching in registers, no removal or reordering); mainly used for memory-mapped I/O.

questions.title: What is a pointer? Explain the concept of a pointer.
questions.answer: A pointer is a variable whose value is the address of another variable. E.g., int a=10; int *b=&a; int c=*b; → b holds a's address (e.g., 4096), c = 10.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A pointer is a variable whose **value is the address** of another variable. `&x` gives an address; `*p` dereferences (accesses the value at that address).

### Code (C)
```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    int a = 10;
    int *b = &a;      /* b holds the address of a */
    int c = *b;       /* c = value stored at that address = 10 */
    printf("b=%p c=%d\n", (void *)b, c);
    *b = 20;          /* modifies a through the pointer */
    printf("a=%d\n", a);   /* 20 */
    return 0;
}
```

| Variable | Address (assumed) | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a | 0x1000 | 10 (later 20) |
| b | 0x2000 | 0x1000 (= 4096) |
| c | 0x2008 | 10 |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  B["b @0x2000 = 0x1000"] -->|"points to"| A["a @0x1000 = 10"]
  C["c = *b = 10"]
```

### Follow-ups
- *Pointer arithmetic?* `p + 1` advances by `sizeof(*p)` bytes.
- *SV analogue?* Class handles (references, no arithmetic) and `ref` arguments.

questions.title: Explain pass by value and pass by reference in C.
questions.answer: Pass by value copies the value into a new local variable – changes don't affect the original (c stays 15). Pass by reference passes the address – changes via the pointer affect the original (c becomes 20).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Pass by value** copies the argument – changes inside the function don't affect the caller. **Pass by reference** (in C: pass a pointer to the variable) lets the function modify the caller's variable and avoids copying large data.

### Code
```c
#include <stdio.h>
void pass_by_value(int a)      { a = a + 5; }        /* modifies local copy */
void pass_by_reference(int *b) { *b = *b + 5; }      /* modifies caller's variable */

int main(void) {
    int c = 15;
    pass_by_value(c);
    printf("1. Value of C is %d\n", c);   /* 15 */
    pass_by_reference(&c);
    printf("2. Value of C is %d\n", c);   /* 20 */
    return 0;
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph ByValue["pass_by_value"]
    C1["c = 15 (caller)"] -->|"copy"| A1["a = 15 → 20 (local)"]
  end
  subgraph ByRef["pass_by_reference"]
    C2["c = 15 → 20"] 
    B2["b = &c"] -->|"*b += 5"| C2
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *Arrays in C?* Decay to pointers – effectively passed by reference.
- *SystemVerilog?* `ref` arguments (automatic tasks/functions), `const ref` for read-only large arrays; class handles are passed by value but refer to the same object.

questions.title: What is the value and size of a NULL pointer?
questions.answer: Value of a NULL pointer is 0; its size equals the pointer size of the machine – 4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 bytes on 64-bit.

questions.title: What is a linked list? How many types of linked lists are there?
questions.answer: A linked list is a group of nodes forming a sequence, each with data and a link to the next node. Types: singly (one-way) linked list and doubly (two-way) linked list (plus circular variants).

questions.title: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search, binary search, insertion sort, merge sort and bucket sort?
questions.answer: Linear search O(N), binary search O(log N), insertion sort O(N^2), merge sort O(N log N); bucket sort worst case O(N^2).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Big-O keeps only the dominant term (5n^4 + 6n^2 + 1 → O(n^4)). Worst cases:

| Algorithm | Worst-case time | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear search | O(N) | may check every element |
| Binary search | O(log N) | halves the sorted range each step |
| Insertion sort | O(N^2) | reverse-sorted input shifts every element |
| Merge sort | O(N log N) | log N levels × N work per level |
| Bucket sort | O(N^2) | all elements in one bucket (average O(N + k)) |

Worked example – binary search for 23 in [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91]:

| Step | low | high | mid | a[mid] | action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | 9 | 4 | 16 | go right |
| 2 | 5 | 9 | 7 | 56 | go left |
| 3 | 5 | 6 | 5 | 23 | found (3 steps ≤ log2 10 + 1) |

### Follow-ups
- *Best case of insertion sort?* O(N) on already-sorted input.

questions.title: What is the space complexity of linear search, binary search, insertion sort, merge sort and bucket sort?
questions.answer: Linear search O(1), binary search O(1), insertion sort O(N), merge sort O(N), bucket sort O(N) (N = list size).

questions.title: Explain the difference between the & and && operators in C/C++.
questions.answer: & is bitwise AND (a=10, b=6 → 2); && is logical AND returning a boolean ((a==10) && (b==6) → true).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `&` is **bitwise AND** (operates on each bit, returns an integer). `&&` is **logical AND** (treats operands as true/false, returns 0/1, and **short-circuits**).

| Expression (a=10, b=6) | Computation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `a & b` | 1010 & 0110 | 0010 = **2** |
| `a && b` | true && true | **1** |
| `(a == 10) && (b == 6)` | 1 && 1 | 1 |
| `1 & 2` | 01 & 10 | 0 (false!) |
| `1 && 2` | true && true | 1 |

### Code
```c
int a = 10, b = 6;
int bw = a & b;                  /* 2 */
int lg = (a == 10) && (b == 6);  /* 1 */
if (p != NULL && p->valid) { }   /* short-circuit protects the dereference */
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `if (flags & MASK == MASK)` parses as `flags & (MASK == MASK)` – parenthesize.
- `&` does not short-circuit: both sides always evaluated.
- Same distinction exists in SystemVerilog (`&` bitwise / `&&` logical, plus unary `&` reduction).

questions.title: How do a structure and a union differ in terms of memory allocation in C/C++?
questions.answer: Structs allocate space for all members sequentially; unions allocate only enough for the largest member and all members share the same space (only one is used at a time).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A **struct** allocates space for **all** members, laid out one after another (plus alignment padding); size ≥ sum of members. A **union** allocates space for its **largest** member only; all members overlay the same bytes, so only one is meaningful at a time.

```c
struct S { int i; char c[8]; };   /* i at offset 0, c at offset 4  → 12 bytes */
union  U { int i; char c[8]; };   /* i and c both at offset 0     →  8 bytes */
```

| Offset | struct S | union U |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–3 | i | i / c[0..3] |
| 4–7 | c[0..3] | c[4..7] |
| 8–11 | c[4..7] | – |
| sizeof | 12 | 8 |

### Explanation
- Unions are used for type punning, variant records, and saving memory; a tag field usually says which member is valid.
- Alignment matters: `struct { char a; int b; }` is 8 bytes, not 5 (3 bytes padding).

### Follow-ups
- *SV equivalents?* `struct packed` / `union packed` – a packed union lets one bit-vector be viewed as different formats (e.g., a bus word as header or payload).

questions.title: How much memory is allocated for struct ID { int IntID; char CharID[8]; }?
questions.answer: 12 bytes (4 for int + 8 for the char array).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A struct holds all members: 4 (int) + 8 (char[8]) = **12 bytes** (no padding needed: char array has 1-byte alignment and 12 is a multiple of int's 4-byte alignment).

| Member | Offset | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| IntID | 0 | 4 |
| CharID[8] | 4 | 8 |
| **Total** | | **12** |

```c
#include <stdio.h>
struct ID { int IntID; char CharID[8]; };
int main(void) { printf("%zu\n", sizeof(struct ID)); return 0; }   /* 12 */
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reorder to `{ char c; int i; }` and padding appears; with `double` members alignment can grow to 8.
- Assumes 4-byte int (typical).

questions.title: How much memory is allocated for union ID { int IntID; char CharID[8]; }?
questions.answer: 8 bytes – memory is allocated only for the largest member (char[8]).

questions.title: What is a stack and how does it differ from a FIFO?
questions.answer: A stack is LIFO (last in first out); a FIFO is first in first out.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Both are ordered buffers. A **stack** is **LIFO** – the last element pushed is the first popped (one access end). A **FIFO/queue** is **first in, first out** – elements leave in arrival order (write at tail, read at head).

| Push order | Stack pop order | FIFO pop order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A, B, C | C, B, A | A, B, C |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Stack
    IN1["push/pop"] <--> TOP["C (top)"] --- B1["B"] --- A1["A"]
  end
  subgraph FIFO
    W["write"] --> T["C"] --> M["B"] --> H["A"] --> R["read"]
  end
```

| Aspect | Stack | FIFO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Order | LIFO | FIFO |
| Pointers | 1 (top) | 2 (read, write) |
| Uses | call stack, expression evaluation, undo | buffering between producer/consumer, clock-domain crossing |

### Follow-ups
- *Hardware FIFO full/empty?* Compare read/write pointers with an extra wrap bit.

questions.title: What is a kernel?
questions.answer: A kernel is a program that manages I/O requests from software and translates them into CPU/hardware instructions – the core of the OS.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** The kernel is the core of an operating system: it manages CPU scheduling, memory, devices and system calls, translating software I/O requests into operations on the hardware.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  U["User applications"] --> SH["Shell / libraries"]
  SH -->|"system calls"| K["Kernel: scheduler, memory manager, file systems, drivers"]
  K --> HW["Hardware: CPU, memory, devices"]
```

| Kernel responsibility | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Process management | scheduling, context switches |
| Memory management | virtual memory, paging |
| Device drivers | disk, network, USB |
| File systems | ext4, NFS |
| System calls | `open`, `read`, `fork` |

### Follow-ups
- *Monolithic vs microkernel?* Linux is monolithic (drivers in kernel space); microkernels move services to user space.

questions.title: What is UNIX and how is it different from Linux?
questions.answer: UNIX is a multi-user, multi-tasking OS made of kernel, shell and programs. Linux is a free, open-source UNIX-like OS (e.g., Ubuntu) while UNIX versions are vendor-licensed (e.g., Solaris).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** UNIX is a family of multi-user, multitasking operating systems (originally AT&T), made of a kernel, a shell and programs; commercial variants are vendor licensed (Solaris, AIX, HP-UX). Linux is a free, open-source, UNIX-like kernel (plus GNU tools = distributions like Ubuntu, RHEL).

| Aspect | UNIX | Linux |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin | AT&T Bell Labs (1969) | Linus Torvalds (1991) |
| License | proprietary per vendor (BSDs open) | GPL, free |
| Development | vendors | open-source community |
| Examples | Solaris, AIX, HP-UX, macOS (certified) | Ubuntu, RHEL/CentOS, Debian |
| Hardware | vendor-specific | almost anything |

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  USER["user"] --> SHELL["shell (bash, csh, tcsh)"] --> KERNEL["kernel"] --> HW["hardware"]
  PROGS["programs/utilities (ls, grep, make)"] --> KERNEL
```

### Follow-ups
- *Why does DV care?* EDA tools run on Linux farms; scripting (shell, Perl/Python), LSF/grid, and file handling are daily work.

questions.title: What does Perl stand for?
questions.answer: Practical Extraction and Reporting Language.

questions.title: Perl is an interpreted language. What does this mean?
questions.answer: Perl translates source statement by statement into intermediate code interpreted by another program rather than producing a binary; it stops at the first error.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Perl source is not compiled to a native binary ahead of time. The `perl` interpreter parses the script into an internal representation (op-tree/intermediate code) and executes it at run time; you run the source directly.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SRC["script.pl"] --> P["perl interpreter: parse → op-tree"] --> RUN["execute ops at run time"]
```

| Aspect | Interpreted (Perl) | Compiled (C) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run | `perl script.pl` | `gcc` then `./a.out` |
| Edit-run cycle | fast | slower |
| Execution speed | slower | faster |
| Portability | wherever perl exists | recompile per platform |
| Errors | syntax errors found when the whole file is parsed; runtime errors when reached | at compile time |

### Follow-ups
- *Detail:* Perl actually compiles the whole file before running (so `use` executes at compile time) – which is why syntax errors anywhere stop the script before it starts.

questions.title: What are the different data types in Perl?
questions.answer: Scalars ($: number, string, or reference), arrays (@: ordered lists of scalars, index from 0), hashes (%: unordered key/value pairs).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Three core types identified by sigils: **scalars** `$` (number, string or reference), **arrays** `@` (ordered list, index from 0), **hashes** `%` (unordered key → value pairs).

### Code
```perl
use strict; use warnings;
my $name  = "fifo_test";              # scalar
my @seeds = (11, 42, 7);              # array
my %res   = (fifo_test => "PASS", axi_test => "FAIL");   # hash

print "$name first seed: $seeds[0]\n";       # element of array is a scalar: $
print "count: ", scalar(@seeds), "\n";       # 3
for my $t (sort keys %res) { print "$t => $res{$t}\n"; }
my $aref = \@seeds;                          # reference (scalar)
print "last: $$aref[-1] / $aref->[-1]\n";
```

| Type | Sigil | Element access | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Scalar | `$` | – | `$x = 5` |
| Array | `@` | `$a[i]` | `@a = (1,2)` |
| Hash | `%` | `$h{key}` | `%h = (k => v)` |

### Follow-ups
- *Nested data?* Use references: `$h{list} = [1,2,3]`, access `@{$h{list}}`.

questions.title: What is a cron job? When would you use one?
questions.answer: A cron job is time-based job scheduling that runs jobs automatically at specified times/intervals, e.g., a script computing per-user disk usage run periodically.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** cron is the UNIX/Linux time-based scheduler. A cron job is a command/script that runs automatically at specified times/intervals, configured in a crontab.

```text
# ┌ min (0-59) ┌ hour (0-23) ┌ day-of-month ┌ month ┌ day-of-week (0=Sun)
# │            │             │              │       │
  0            2             *              *       *    /proj/scripts/nightly_regress.sh >> /proj/logs/nightly.log 2>&1
  */30         *             *              *       1-5  /proj/scripts/disk_usage.pl
```

| Field | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0 2 * * *` | nightly | 02:00 every day |
| `*/30 * * * 1-5` | every 30 min | weekdays |
| `0 9 * * 1` | weekly | Monday 09:00 |

### Explanation
- Edit with `crontab -e`, list with `crontab -l`.
- DV uses: nightly regressions, coverage merges, disk-usage reports, cleanup of old sim directories.

### Follow-ups
- *Pitfall?* cron runs with a minimal environment – source your setup (PATH, licenses) inside the script.

questions.title: What is the use of the rsync command in UNIX/Linux?
questions.answer: rsync (remote sync) copies/synchronizes files across disks, networks and machines, transferring only changed portions with compression; used for backups and mirroring.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `rsync` (remote sync) copies/synchronizes files and directories locally or across machines, transferring **only the changed parts** (delta algorithm), optionally compressed – ideal for backups and mirroring.

### Code
```bash
# mirror a regression result tree to a backup server, preserving attributes
rsync -avz --delete /proj/regress/ backup:/archive/regress/
# dry run first to see what would change
rsync -avzn --exclude '*.vpd' /proj/regress/ backup:/archive/regress/
```

| Option | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `-a` | archive: recursive, preserve perms/times/links |
| `-v` | verbose |
| `-z` | compress during transfer |
| `-n` | dry run |
| `--delete` | delete files at destination that no longer exist at source |
| `--exclude` | skip patterns |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Trailing slash matters: `src/` copies contents, `src` copies the directory itself.

### Follow-ups
- *rsync vs scp?* scp copies everything every time; rsync only differences and can resume.

questions.title: True or false: variable names in C can contain alphanumeric characters as well as special characters.
questions.answer: False – C variable names may contain only letters, digits and underscore (not starting with a digit).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **False.** C identifiers may contain only letters, digits and the underscore `_`; they cannot start with a digit and cannot be keywords. Special characters like `$`, `@`, `-`, `#` are not allowed (some compilers accept `$` as an extension).

| Identifier | Valid? | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `count_1` | yes | letters, digit, underscore |
| `_tmp` | yes (reserved-ish at file scope) | leading underscore allowed |
| `1st_val` | no | starts with a digit |
| `data-out` | no | `-` is an operator |
| `rate$` | no (standard C) | `$` not portable |
| `int` | no | keyword |

### Follow-ups
- *SystemVerilog?* Simple identifiers may contain letters, digits, `_` and `$` (not first); escaped identifiers `\bus[0] ` allow any printable chars.

questions.title: What is the use of the '\0' character in C/C++?
questions.answer: It is the terminating null character marking the end of a string.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `'\0'` (NUL, value 0) is the **string terminator**: C strings are char arrays that end at the first `'\0'`. All `str*` functions rely on it.

```c
char s[] = "DV";        /* stored as 'D' 'V' '\0' → sizeof(s) == 3, strlen(s) == 2 */
```

| Index | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| s[i] | 'D' (0x44) | 'V' (0x56) | '\0' (0x00) |

### Code
```c
size_t my_strlen(const char *s) {
    size_t n = 0;
    while (s[n] != '\0') n++;   /* stop at the terminator */
    return n;
}
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Forgetting space for `'\0'` (e.g., `char buf[2] = "DV";` in C has no terminator) → buffer overruns.
- `strncpy` doesn't always terminate.

questions.title: What are binary trees?
