questions.answer: Binary trees extend linked lists: each node has a left and a right pointer, each of which can branch to further nodes.

questions.title: How can you generate random numbers in C?
questions.answer: Use the rand() function from <stdlib.h> (seeded with srand()).

questions.title: What are special characters, quantifiers and anchors in regular expressions?
questions.answer: Special characters are meta-characters with special meaning (\, ^, $, (), [], |). Quantifiers specify how often to match (*, +, ?, {}). Anchors specify where to match (^, $, <, >).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Special (meta) characters** have syntactic meaning; **quantifiers** say *how many times* the preceding item matches; **anchors** say *where* the match must occur (they match positions, not characters).

| Category | Tokens | Example | Matches |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Special chars | `\ . ^ $ ( ) [ ] { } \| * + ?` | `a\.b` | literal "a.b" |
| Character class | `[abc]`, `[^0-9]`, `\d \w \s` | `[0-9a-f]+` | hex digits |
| Quantifiers | `*` (0+), `+` (1+), `?` (0/1), `{n}`, `{n,m}` | `x{2,3}` | xx, xxx |
| Anchors | `^` (line start), `$` (line end), `\b` (word boundary), `\<` `\>` (word start/end in grep/vim) | `^ERROR` | ERROR only at line start |

### Code (Perl)
```perl
while (my $line = <STDIN>) {
    # anchor ^, special (), quantifiers + and ?
    if ($line =~ /^UVM_ERROR\s+(\S+)\((\d+)\)\s*@\s*(\d+)/) {
        print "file=$1 line=$2 time=$3\n";
    }
}
```

### Follow-ups
- *Escape a metacharacter?* Prefix with backslash: `\$`, `\(`.

questions.title: What is the difference between a class and an object?
questions.answer: A class is a set of attributes and behavior grouped together; an object is an instance of the class representing a real entity (e.g., animal class; dog, cat objects).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A **class** is a blueprint/type defining data members (attributes) and methods (behavior). An **object** is a concrete **instance** of the class created at run time with its own copy of the data.

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class animal;
  string name;
  int    legs;
  function new(string name, int legs); this.name = name; this.legs = legs; endfunction
  function void speak(); $display("%s has %0d legs", name, legs); endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    animal dog = new("dog", 4);   // object 1
    animal bird = new("bird", 2); // object 2
    dog.speak(); bird.speak();
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class animal {
    string name
    int legs
    new(name, legs)
    speak()
  }
```

| | Class | Object |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What | type definition | instance in memory |
| When | compile time | created at run time (`new`) |
| How many | one definition | many instances |

### Follow-ups
- *SV handle vs object?* `animal a;` is just a null handle; the object exists only after `a = new(...)`.

questions.title: What is the difference between a class and a struct in C++?
questions.answer: In C++ the only real difference is default access: class members are private by default, struct members public by default.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** In C++ they are almost identical (both can have members, methods, constructors, inheritance). The only language difference: **members and base classes are private by default in a class, public by default in a struct**.

```cpp
struct PointS { int x, y; };          // x, y public by default
class  PointC { int x, y; };          // x, y private by default

int main() {
    PointS s; s.x = 1;                // OK
    PointC c; // c.x = 1;             // error: 'int PointC::x' is private
}
```

| Aspect | struct | class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default member access | public | private |
| Default inheritance | public | private |
| Convention | plain data (POD) | encapsulated types with invariants |

### Follow-ups
- *Can a struct have virtual functions?* Yes in C++.

questions.title: What is the difference between a class and a struct in SystemVerilog?
questions.answer: In SV a struct is an integral type allocated when declared; a class is a dynamic type – declaring it gives a null handle and memory is allocated only when an object is created.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A SV **struct** is an integral/value type – memory is allocated when it is declared, assignment copies the data, no methods. A **class** is a dynamic reference type – declaring it gives a **null handle**; memory is allocated only by `new()`; it supports methods, inheritance, polymorphism, randomization with `rand`.

### Code
```systemverilog
typedef struct packed { logic [7:0] addr; logic [31:0] data; } pkt_s;

class pkt_c;
  rand bit [7:0]  addr;
  rand bit [31:0] data;
  function void print(); $display("addr=%h data=%h", addr, data); endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  pkt_s s1, s2;      // storage exists already
  pkt_c c1, c2;      // null handles
  initial begin
    s1.addr = 8'h10; s2 = s1; s2.addr = 8'h20;   // s1.addr still 10 (copy)
    c1 = new(); c1.addr = 8'h10;
    c2 = c1;   c2.addr = 8'h20;                  // c1.addr is now 20 (same object)
  end
endmodule
```

| Aspect | struct | class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | value (integral if packed) | reference (handle) |
| Allocation | at declaration | at `new()` |
| Assignment | copies data | copies handle |
| Methods / inheritance | no | yes |
| Synthesizable | yes (packed) | no |

### Follow-ups
- *Can structs contain rand fields?* Yes, inside a class: `rand pkt_s s;`.

questions.title: What are public, private and protected members of a class?
questions.answer: Private members are accessible only within the class (not derived classes); public members are accessible inside and outside the class and in derived classes; protected members are accessible within the class and derived classes but not outside.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Access qualifiers control visibility. **Public**: accessible everywhere. **Private** (`local` in SV): only inside the class itself, not derived classes. **Protected**: inside the class **and derived classes**, not outside.

| Accessed from | public | protected | private / `local` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Same class | yes | yes | yes |
| Derived class | yes | yes | **no** |
| Outside code | yes | **no** | **no** |

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class base;
  int            pub_cnt;       // public (default in SV)
  protected int  prot_cnt;
  local int      priv_cnt;      // 'local' = private
endclass

class derived extends base;
  function void f();
    pub_cnt++;      // OK
    prot_cnt++;     // OK - protected visible in derived
    // priv_cnt++;  // compile error - local
  endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    derived d = new();
    d.pub_cnt = 1;     // OK
    // d.prot_cnt = 1; // error - not visible outside
  end
endmodule
```

### Follow-ups
- *Default access in SV vs C++?* SV class members are public by default; C++ class members are private.

questions.title: What is polymorphism?
questions.answer: Polymorphism: ability of an entity to refer to objects of various classes at run time; achieved via inheritance and virtual functions in SV (and overloading in C++); the method of the actual object type is called.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Polymorphism ("many forms") lets one handle/interface refer to objects of different classes and invoke the **right method for the actual object type at run time**. In SystemVerilog this comes from inheritance + `virtual` methods; C++ adds compile-time polymorphism (function/operator overloading, templates).

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class shape;
  virtual function real area(); return 0; endfunction
endclass
class square extends shape;
  real s; function new(real s); this.s = s; endfunction
  virtual function real area(); return s*s; endfunction
endclass
class circle extends shape;
  real r; function new(real r); this.r = r; endfunction
  virtual function real area(); return 3.14159*r*r; endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    shape list[$];
    square sq = new(2.0); circle ci = new(1.0);
    list.push_back(sq); list.push_back(ci);
    foreach (list[i]) $display("area=%f", list[i].area());  // 4.0, 3.14 - dynamic dispatch
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
classDiagram
  shape <|-- square
  shape <|-- circle
  class shape { +area() virtual }
  class square { +area() }
  class circle { +area() }
```

### Follow-ups
- *UVM use?* Factory overrides: a test replaces `base_driver` with `err_driver`; the env still calls through base handles.
- *What if `area` weren't virtual?* The base-class version would be called (static binding on handle type).

questions.title: What are method overriding and method overloading, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: Overloading: same function name defined multiple times with different parameters (e.g., add(int,int), add(int,int,int), add(float,float)). Overriding: derived class redefines a base-class virtual method. SV supports only overriding.

questions.title: What is operator overloading?
questions.answer: Operator overloading is redefining built-in operators for user-defined types (polymorphism); supported in C++, not SV. E.g., overload + to add data members of two Testclass objects.

questions.title: What is a constructor method?
questions.answer: A constructor is a special member function invoked automatically when an object is created; in C++ it has the class name, in SV it is new().

questions.title: What is a destructor?
questions.answer: A destructor is invoked automatically when an object goes out of scope; C++: class name with ~ prefix. SV has no destructor (automatic garbage collection).

questions.title: What is the difference between composition and inheritance in OOP?
questions.answer: Composition is a 'has-a' relationship (a class instantiates another class's object, e.g., ford has an engine); inheritance is an 'is-a' relationship (ford derives from car).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Inheritance** = "is-a" (a `ford` **is a** `car`; it derives from the base class). **Composition** = "has-a" (a `ford` **has an** `engine` object as a member).

```mermaid
classDiagram
  car <|-- ford : is-a (inheritance)
  ford *-- engine : has-a (composition)
  class car { +drive() }
  class ford { +engine e }
  class engine { +start() }
```

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class engine; function void start(); $display("vroom"); endfunction endclass
class car;    virtual function void drive(); $display("driving"); endfunction endclass

class ford extends car;        // is-a
  engine e;                    // has-a
  function new(); e = new(); endfunction
  virtual function void drive(); e.start(); super.drive(); endfunction
endclass
```

| Aspect | Inheritance | Composition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relation | is-a | has-a |
| Coupling | tight (depends on base internals) | loose |
| Reuse | extends behavior | delegates to contained object |
| UVM example | `my_driver extends uvm_driver` | env **has** agents, agent **has** driver/monitor |

### Follow-ups
- *Guideline?* "Favor composition over inheritance" unless there's a true is-a relation.

questions.title: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy in object-oriented programming?
questions.answer: Shallow copy: new object with copied values, but references to other objects copy only the handle. Deep copy: referenced objects' values are also copied, not just handles.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** **Shallow copy** creates a new object and copies the member values; for members that are handles to other objects, **only the handle is copied** – both copies share the sub-object. **Deep copy** also recursively copies the referenced objects, so the copies are fully independent.

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class A; int a, b; endclass

class B;
  int x;
  A   objA;
  function new(); objA = new(); endfunction
  function B deep_copy();
    deep_copy = new();          // new B with its own new A
    deep_copy.x = x;
    deep_copy.objA.a = objA.a;  // copy contents, not the handle
    deep_copy.objA.b = objA.b;
  endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    B b1 = new(), b2, b3;
    b1.objA.a = 5;
    b2 = new b1;            // SHALLOW: b2.objA == b1.objA (same object)
    b3 = b1.deep_copy();    // DEEP: separate A
    b1.objA.a = 9;
    $display("%0d %0d", b2.objA.a, b3.objA.a);   // 9 5
  end
endmodule
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Shallow
    B1["b1"] --> A1["A (a=9)"]
    B2["b2"] --> A1
  end
  subgraph Deep
    B1d["b1"] --> A1d["A (a=9)"]
    B3["b3"] --> A3["A copy (a=5)"]
  end
```

### Follow-ups
- *In UVM?* Implement `do_copy()` to deep-copy nested objects; `clone()` = create + copy.

questions.title: What are virtual functions in C++ or other OOP languages?
questions.answer: A virtual function is declared in a base class with the virtual keyword and can be redefined in a derived class (method overriding); calls dispatch based on the object's actual type.

questions.title: What is meant by multiple inheritance?
questions.answer: Multiple inheritance lets a class inherit from more than one parent class; C++ supports it, SystemVerilog does not (single inheritance only).
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Multiple inheritance lets a class derive from **more than one parent class**, inheriting members of all. C++ supports it; SystemVerilog classes support only **single** inheritance (SV-2012 adds `interface class` + `implements` for multiple *interfaces*).

```mermaid
classDiagram
  Printer <|-- MultiFunction
  Scanner <|-- MultiFunction
  class Printer { +print() }
  class Scanner { +scan() }
```

### Code
```cpp
class Printer { public: void print() {} };
class Scanner { public: void scan()  {} };
class MultiFunction : public Printer, public Scanner {};   // C++ multiple inheritance
```
```systemverilog
interface class printable; pure virtual function void print(); endclass
interface class scannable; pure virtual function void scan();  endclass
class multi_function implements printable, scannable;       // SV-2012
  virtual function void print(); endfunction
  virtual function void scan();  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Diamond problem: two parents share a grandparent → ambiguity/duplicate base; C++ uses `virtual` inheritance to fix.

### Follow-ups
- *Single inheritance?* Exactly one parent (SV `extends`).

questions.title: What is an abstract class?
questions.answer: An abstract class has one or more abstract (declared, unimplemented) methods and cannot be instantiated; subclasses implement them. In SV, use 'virtual class' (e.g., virtual class BaseShape with get_num_edges implemented in Rectangle).

questions.title: What are static methods inside a class?
questions.answer: Static methods are declared with the static keyword and can be used without creating an object; only one copy is shared by all objects.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** A static method belongs to the **class**, not to an object: callable without creating an instance (`ClassName::method()`), only one copy shared by all objects, and it can access only static members (no `this`).

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class packet;
  static int count;          // shared by all packets
  int id;
  function new(); id = count++; endfunction
  static function int get_count();   // no 'this' available
    return count;
  endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    packet p1 = new(), p2 = new();
    $display("%0d", packet::get_count());   // 2 - called on the class
  end
endmodule
```

| Aspect | Static method | Instance method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Needs object | no | yes |
| Access to non-static members | no | yes |
| `this` | not available | available |
| Typical use | factories, singletons, counters, utilities | object behavior |

### Follow-ups
- *UVM:* `type_id::create()`, `uvm_config_db#(T)::set/get`, `uvm_root::get()` are static methods.
- *Static method vs method with static lifetime?* `static function` (class-level) differs from `function static` (static variables inside).

questions.title: What is the 'this' pointer with reference to a class?
questions.answer: 'this' is a special pointer/handle referencing the current object of a class inside the class scope.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** `this` is an implicit handle/pointer to the **current object** inside its non-static methods – used to disambiguate members from same-named arguments, or to pass the object itself to another function.

### Code (SystemVerilog)
```systemverilog
class packet;
  bit [7:0] addr;
  function new(bit [7:0] addr);
    this.addr = addr;          // member = argument
  endfunction
  function void register(ref packet q[$]);
    q.push_back(this);         // pass self
  endfunction
endclass
```
```cpp
class Packet { int addr; public: Packet(int addr) { this->addr = addr; } };  // C++: pointer, so ->
```

| Language | Form |
| --- | --- |
| C++ | pointer: `this->x`, `*this` |
| SystemVerilog | handle: `this.x` |
| Static methods | `this` not allowed |

### Follow-ups
- *UVM:* `super.new(name, parent)` and passing `this` as parent when creating child components: `drv = my_driver::type_id::create("drv", this);`

questions.title: What is type conversion and type casting in programming languages?
questions.answer: Both change one data type to another: type conversion is implicit (compiler does it, e.g., assigning float to int), type casting is explicit by the programmer.
questions.solution:
**Key idea:** Both change a value from one type to another. **Type conversion** is **implicit** (done automatically by the compiler, e.g., float assigned to int). **Type casting** is **explicit** (the programmer requests it).

### Code
```c
float f = 3.75;
int   i = f;            /* implicit conversion: truncates to 3 */
int   j = (int)f;       /* explicit cast: 3 */
double d = (double)7 / 2;   /* cast before divide → 3.5 instead of 3 */
```
```systemverilog
real r = 3.75;
int  i = r;                 // implicit: rounds to 4 in SV (real→int rounds!)
int  j = int'(r);           // static cast: 4
int  k = $rtoi(r);          // truncate: 3
typedef enum {RED, GREEN} color_e;
color_e c;
initial if (!$cast(c, 1)) $error("bad enum");   // dynamic cast with check
```

| Kind | Who | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Implicit conversion | compiler | `int i = f;` |
| Static cast | programmer, compile time | `(int)f`, `int'(r)` |
| Dynamic cast | programmer, checked at run time | `$cast(child_h, base_h)` |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- C truncates float→int; SystemVerilog rounds real→int on assignment.
- `$cast` for class handles fails if the object isn't actually of the target type.
